items.body: 会場：画廊 BananaMoon［長野県］ 会期：2026/06/12〜2026/07/12 公式サイト：https://www.instagram.com/p/DZXGTPLT1ht/ ［筆者撮影］ 別の風景から話し始める。 薄暗い展示室で、壁にかかる額装された山の絵を端から見ていく。さまざまな筆致の山が並ぶ。 その部屋ではじめから視野に入っていた一枚に至る。 キャンバスの右下から上方へ尾根が走っている。尾根の右側斜面は山自身によって影が落ちていて、左側は岩肌と緑が入り混じっている。その入り混じりはきれいに生え際がわかるのでもなく、光を受けて煌めく白、暗がりの黒み、まわりの色を吸った残雪のような淡い水色、添えられる黄緑……。言葉を充てられない色の織り混ざりや、漠然と明るい斜面とはこうである、といつか登った山の眺めと頭のなかで突き合わせる。明るさに目を細めたあと、視線を上げた向こう──画面の上部──には、空の青にぼやけて溶け込みそうな山並みが横切っている。淡いが、その中に明暗がある。より遠くにあるだろうその山の方が、ありありと触るように形がわかる。遠くの山の淡さが、先程の明るい斜面につながっていることに気づく。奥へ向かった目が戻ってくる。横切る山の稜線が影と光の境につながっている。薄暗がりの斜面は、手前では明るく、さまざまな色で光っている。 光り、明るい斜面は緑の一色になり、キャンバスの左下へ谷が滑り落ちていく。どこまでも滑り落ちていかないよう、もうひとつの暗い影の斜面が緑をせき止める。底に、ポツポツと明るさがまだ残されている。 それは確かに山であったし、同時に油絵の、筆が走った跡でもあった。暗がりも、明るさも、淡さも、数センチ幅のストロークの中にある。山頂から眺め下ろしたときの、普段よりはるかに遠くまで細やかにきらきらと光って見通せる感覚が蘇る。動いた筆が想像されるのと同時に、このことは思い出されるし、見えている。近づけば筆致が見えてくる、というわけでもない。遠目のときからそれはストロークの集まりだったし、近づいてもまだ山肌だった。 ここからここまでがこの山、とは言えない分け難さに、目がぐるぐるとキャンバスの上を巡り続ける。そのうち、再び、明暗のはっきり分かれた尾根に戻ってきた。ストロークの方向は、私には厳密にわからない。だが、その尾根を境に分かれていることはわかる。油絵のわずかな絵の具の盛り上がりがその際を描き出している。色の分かれ目だけでなく、絵の具の斜面にまた、明暗がある。この、際の暗がりと煌めきの確からしさが、この絵を山たらしめていた。私の目は、そこまで見て取ることがもうできている。 山岳画家・上田太郎の《西穂高岳頂上より 焼岳、乗鞍岳、上高地を望む》（1994）を収める安曇野山岳美術館のすぐ近く、同じ山裾に画家・成瀬政博の私設した画廊BananaMoonがある。入口の扉を開き、細い廊下を進み数段の階段を下りると、アーティスト・内田涼の個展「水を咬む」が始まっていた。 縦横に加えて高さの寸法も等しく、キューブに近い展示室の壁沿いにぐるりと絵が掛けられている。ひとつ目、二つ目、三つ目とまわり、四つ目の壁との間に2階へ上がる階段がある（階段の先、2階では絵画を中心とした成瀬のりこ展「どうやろ」が行なわれている）。それぞれの壁には三枚ずつ絵が掛けられている。そして、四つ目の壁の中央には人がひとり通れるだけの入口があり、中の小部屋では三面に一枚ずつ絵が掛けられている。振り返ると入口越しにひとつ目の壁に掛かった絵が見える。 小部屋の中から二つ目の壁を見る。展示室に入室したときに最初に見える絵もこの三点である。ナンバリングに則り、右から順に《frequently (頻繁に) transparent (透明な) 》《eventually (やがて) again (ふたたび) 》《二 (五) 羽》。すべて2026年に制作された新作［筆者撮影］ 内田の絵画は自身のステートメントに「絵具の垂れや滲みによって生じた形を起点に構築していく絵画作品を中心に制作を行う。／偶然性や他者性といった不確定要素を取り込みながら、形態に宿るイメージの解体や再構成を目指す。」と書いているように、キャンバスには具体的なモチーフを感じさせない形が並び、その一つひとつに刷毛の太さと移動が想像される。グラフィックデザインも手がける内田は、色の滲みを含んだストロークの輪郭だけコピー&ペーストしたように単色の塗りつぶしで再配置したり、縁を黒々とした線でなぞって輪郭を強調したりする。塗りつぶしから、滲んだ表現まで自在に質感を変化させられるアクリル絵の具の特性が活かされており、抽象的な形に実際の描画の手順とは異なる重なりや運動を想像させることが特徴である。 今回の個展の起点は、このキャンバスと絵の具の関係にある。内田は本展に寄せたテキストで「水と絵の具が、まるで何者かに『咬まれている』ような表情をみせた。手違いで発注した新しいキャンバス布は表面に油が乗っていて、いつものように滲んでくれない。」と書き始める。そして、「大きな刷毛を滑らせた瞬間から次々と水分をはじいていく。それはとがりすぎず鈍すぎない牙がゆっくりと食い込んでいくような仕方で、知っているような知らないような、見たことがあるような無いような様子で、眺めている時間は幸福だった。」とここに並ぶ絵に起きた出来事、そしてそれを眺めた経験について述べている。テキストは「『水』という名詞と『咬む』という動詞が接近したのは、偶然的でとても美しいことだった。」と、絵を介して自身の実感に言葉が与えられたことで締められている。この名詞と動詞の接近は、13点ある展示作品のタイトルが一作を除いて、一見無関係な名詞／動詞／副詞／形容詞を二つ並べたものになったことにも関係しているだろう。 確かに滲んでいるというより弾かれてキャンバス上を滴ったり、わずかに流れたような跡が見られる。その跡は「不確定要素」であるが、内田が刷毛で絵の具を滑らせることで始まったことで、その根元の線の連なりにははっきりと意志がある。 《smooth (滑らかな) rough (ざらざらした) #1》（2026）の右上。キャンバス上で絵の具が弾かれた跡が、キャンバス面のさまざまな透け方からわかる［筆者撮影］ 弾かれたり、滲んだり、塗りつぶしたり、種々のストロークが画面の上に引かれている。私の目は自ずとそのストロークを追い、その幅の端、ほかなる色と接する際を辿る。明確なモチーフを持たない内田の絵画だが、弾かれた絵の具の連なりは、CTスキャンされた内臓の襞のようでも、鉱石の断面のようでも、川の流路のようでもある。はたまた地層のようでもあり、アクリル絵の具の1ミリにも満たない厚みの中で、目はありえる何かのさまざまなスケールでの凹凸を想像してしまう。想像をつい喩えの名詞で挙げてしまったものの、実際想像されているのはそれらを撫でることや歩くこと──動詞なのかもしれなかった。そうして動くことに、形容詞と副詞はまつわっている。作品タイトルをそのとおりに受け取るかは問題ではなく、そのように絵を見ることを介して言葉が立ち現われることへの信が書かれ／描かれていた。 これらの絵を見たあと、あの山の絵を見た。そして、車へ乗り込む前、木々の向こうを横切る筑摩山地を見た。薄曇りの空と山の稜線は同じような色彩のわずかな濃淡差として見えていた。 鑑賞日：2026/07/12（日）

items.body: Psilocybin-assisted therapy for major depressive disorder: Perspective from meta-analysis - PubMedThis meta-analysis indicates that standard-dose psilocybin mapubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov タイトル Psilocybin-assisted therapy for major depressive disorder: Perspective from meta-analysis （日本語訳：大うつ病性障害に対するシロシビン補助療法：メタ解析からの視点）著者 Taro Kishi（岸太郎）、Kenji Sakuma（佐久間健二）、Masakazu Hatano（波多野将一）、Hiroyuki Uchida（内田裕之）、Nakao Iwata（岩田仲生）ら掲載誌 Journal of Affective Disorders（感情障害学雑誌） 2026年8月1日発行（電子公開：2026年3月22日） DOI: 10.1016/j.jad.2026.121675 PMID: 41876058これは6件のランダム化比較試験（RCT）を対象とした系統的レビューとメタ解析で、大うつ病性障害（MDD）に対するシロシビン治療の有効性と安全性の時間的変化を調べた研究です。アブストラクトの正確な日本語訳目的 6件のランダム化比較試験を対象としたこの系統的レビューとメタ解析は、大うつ病性障害（MDD）に対するシロシビン治療の有効性と安全性の時間的変化を調べることを目的とした。方法 標準用量のシロシビン（1回あたり25 mg、または体重70 kgあたり20～30 mg）と低用量のシロシビン（1回あたり10 mg、または体重70 kgあたり15.05 mg）のサブグループごとに、別々にメタ解析を実施した。対照条件はプラセボ、待機リスト対照、ナイアシン、またはシロシビン1 mgであった。結果 標準用量のシロシビンは、うつ症状の軽減において対照群より優れていた（標準化平均差［SMD］：−1.05；95%信頼区間［CI］：−1.60 ～ −0.50、p = 0.0002、I² = 75%、K = 4）。待機リスト対照を含む研究を除外した感度分析では、かなりの異質性を伴わずに標準用量シロシビンの優越性が支持された（SMD：−0.70；95% CI：−1.03 ～ −0.36、p < 0.0001、I² = 43%、K = 2）。この感度分析には、マニュアル化されたシロシビン補助精神療法を組み込んだ2件の二重盲検試験が含まれていた。対照群と比較して、標準用量シロシビンは治療後2～3週時点での反応率（リスク比［RR］：2.34；95% CI：1.52–3.60、p = 0.0001、I² = 0%）および寛解率（RR：3.38；95% CI：1.88–6.08、p < 0.0001、I² = 0%）が高く、治療後6～12週時点での反応率も高かった（RR：2.61；95% CI：1.45–4.71、p = 0.001、I² = 0%）。さらに、標準用量シロシビンは対照群に比べてあらゆる理由による中止率が低かった（RR：0.39；95% CI：0.18–0.87、p = 0.02、I² = 0%）。標準用量シロシビンは、治療後1～9日以内の頭痛（RR：2.06；95% CI：1.11–3.81、p = 0.02、I² = 57%）および悪心（RR：10.20；95% CI：3.80–27.39、p < 0.0001、I² = 0%）の発生率が高かったが、これらの症状はこの期間を過ぎると消失した。低用量シロシビンは、対照群と比較して優越した有効性を示さなかった。 このメタ解析は、標準用量のシロシビンがMDD治療の有望な選択肢となり得ることを示している。しかしながら、今後の研究では、現行の試験間に存在するかなりの方法論的異質性に対処する必要がある。キーワード Depression（うつ病）、Meta-analysis（メタ解析）、Psilocybin（シロシビン）、Randomized controlled trial（ランダム化比較試験）、Systematic review（系統的レビュー）続きをみる

base）」として使いながら外の世界を探索することを発見しました。安全基地とは、安心して探索に出かける出発点であり、不安を感じたときに戻れる避難所のことです。・エインスワースは「ストレンジ・シチュエーション法」という実験手法を開発し、養育者との分離・再会時の1歳児の反応を観察することで、愛着のパターンを類型化しました。当初は「安定型（Bタイプ）」「不安－回避型（Aタイプ）」「不安－両価型／抵抗型（Cタイプ）」の3つに分類され、後にメインとソロモンによって「無秩序型（Dタイプ）」が追加されています。・成人の愛着を測定する方法としては、メインらが開発した「成人愛着面接（AAI）」や、自己報告式の質問紙（ECR尺度など）が代表的です。・現在、心理学者・カウンセラーの間では、大人の愛着スタイルは大きく次の4つに分類されるのが一般的です。 1）安定型（secure） 2）不安型／とらわれ型（anxious-preoccupied） 3）回避型／拒絶型（avoidant-dismissive） 4）恐れ・回避型／無秩序型（fearful-avoidant / disorganized）・不安型・回避型・恐れ回避型はまとめて「不安定愛着（insecure attachment）」と呼ばれます。────────────────────2．不安型愛着スタイルとは────────────────────不安型愛着（anxious attachment、不安型愛着障害とも呼ばれる）は、対人関係において「親密になりたい」という強い欲求と、「見捨てられるのではないか」という強い不安が同時に存在する愛着パターンです。子どもの発達心理学では「不安－両価型（アンビバレント型）」と呼ばれ、養育者との分離時に激しく取り乱す一方、再会しても素直に安心できず、怒りや抵抗を示すことが特徴とされています。見知らぬ人に対する不信感も強い傾向があります。大人になってからは、次のような心理として現れます。・パートナーや友人に愛されているかどうかを常に気にしてしまう・見捨てられること・拒絶されることへの強い恐怖・自己肯定感の低さ、自分は愛される価値がないという感覚・他者からの承認がないと自分の価値を実感できない・共依存的な関係になりやすい・関係が終わることに対して激しい苦痛を感じるこれは「性格の問題」ではなく、幼少期の養育環境によって形成された「心のパターン（内的作業モデル）」であり、意志の弱さとは関係がないという点は、多くの専門家が強調しているポイントです。────────────────────3．不安型愛着が形成される原因────────────────────不安型愛着の中心にあるのは「一貫しない（inconsistent）養育」です。具体的には次のような要因が指摘されています。・親の対応にムラがある あるときは優しく応答し、あるときは無視・拒絶するというように、養育者の態度が気分や状況によってコロコロ変わると、子どもは「どうすれば愛情を得られるのか」がわからなくなり、常に相手の顔色をうかがうようになります。・親自身のメンタルや育児方針が不安定 親のメンタルヘルスの波や、過干渉と放任を繰り返すような養育スタイルも、子どもが安心できる基盤を持てない一因になるとされています。・親の離婚・死別などによる愛情の喪失 幼少期に十分な愛情を受けていたにもかかわらず、離婚や死別などで突然その関係が失われると、「もっと一緒にいてほしい」「もっと自分を見てほしい」という欲求が強く残り、不安型のもとになることがあります。・世代間の連鎖 親自身が愛着に課題を抱えていると、子どもの泣く・笑う・求めるといったサインに適切に応答することが難しくなり、結果として子どもも不安定な愛着スタイルを形成しやすくなります。愛着の傾向は言葉で教えられるものではなく、身近な人との関わりの中で体感的に学習されるため、親に自覚がないまま世代を超えて引き継がれることもあります。ただし、この連鎖は断ち切ることができるとも指摘されています。・脳の発達との関連 子どもの脳は「愛着形成期」に、愛情・安全・親密さがどのように機能するかという内的な設計図（内的作業モデル）を作り上げていきます。研究では、不安型愛着を持つ人は、拒絶や感情的な距離のサインに直面したとき、脳の脅威検知の中枢である「扁桃体」の活動が高まりやすいことが示されています。────────────────────4．不安型愛着の主な特徴（チェックリスト）────────────────────以下は複数の専門機関・カウンセラーが挙げている、不安型愛着に典型的な特徴です。いくつか当てはまるからといって「異常」というわけではなく、あくまで傾向を知るための目安として捉えてください。・相手の表情や声のトーンのわずかな変化に過敏に反応する・LINEやメッセージの返信が遅いと、強い不安や怒りを感じる・「嫌われたかもしれない」という考えが頭から離れなくなる・「自分は愛される価値がない」と感じることがある・人の誘いを断れない、相手に逆らえない・SNSの「いいね」やコメントの数が気になる・褒められないと落ち込みやすく、何度もアピールしてしまう・人をすぐ好きになりやすい（恋愛モードに入りやすい）・友人・恋人など特定の相手に依存しやすい・恋人に何度も愛情を確かめてしまう（試し行動）・一人でいる時間が極端に苦手で、常に誰かとつながっていたい・相手に尽くしすぎて、後から強く疲弊してしまう・気持ちを率直に伝えられず、遠回しな態度で察してほしいと思う・関係が安定すると、逆にそれを壊したくなる衝動を感じることがある・嫉妬心が強く、パートナーの一挙一動が気になる英語圏の心理学系メディアでも同様に、自己肯定感の低さ、批判への過敏さ、一人の時間を過ごすことの難しさ、他者を信頼することの難しさ、強い嫉妬心などが繰り返し挙げられています。────────────────────5．恋愛関係での現れ方────────────────────不安型愛着は、恋愛関係において特に顕著に現れるとされています。・追いかける側になりやすい パートナーが少しでも距離を取ろうとすると、不安が一気に強まり、連絡を増やす・相手を問い詰める・過剰に謝るといった「追いかける」行動（プロテスト行動）に出やすくなります。・不安型×回避型の悪循環 恋愛関係でよく見られる組み合わせが「不安型×回避型」です。不安型は近づくことで安心を得ようとし、回避型は近づかれることで自立が脅かされると感じます。不安型が近づこうとするほど回避型は距離を取りたくなり、回避型が離れるほど不安型はさらに強く追いかけたくなる、という悪循環（いわゆる pursue-withdraw／追う－逃げるダンス）が生まれやすいのです。トリガー（きっかけ）→警報→抗議行動（しがみつき・批判）→一時的な安心→また繰り返す、というループになりやすいと説明されています。・試し行動 「本当に自分を大切に思ってくれているか」を無意識に確認するための行動（連絡を絶ってみる、わざと冷たくするなど）が出ることがあります。これは相手を困らせたいのではなく、「不安を和らげたい」「安心したい」という気持ちから生じるとされています。・理想化しやすい 交際初期に相手を過度に理想化しやすく、外見・性格ともに「かけがえのない存在」として強く思い込む傾向があるとの指摘もあります。・支配的・嫉妬深くなりやすい 研究では、不安型（とらわれ型）の大人はパートナーに対してより支配的になりやすく、嫉妬心も強くなりやすい傾向が報告されています。一方で性的な欲求（リビドー）が安定型・回避型よりも高い傾向があるとする研究もあります。・毒になる関係にはまりやすいリスク 常に強い関心・注目を求める傾向が、交際初期にカリスマ的な魅力を見せるナルシシストや依存症を抱える相手に引き寄せられやすくする、という指摘もあります。関係の初期段階が過ぎたあと、相手がその「愛されたい欲求」を利用し、注目を与えたり奪ったりすることで支配しようとするケースもあるとされます。────────────────────6．友人関係・職場・SNSでの現れ方────────────────────不安型愛着の影響は恋愛関係に限りません。・友人関係：誘いを断れない、嫌われることを恐れて本音を言えない、グループの中で常に周囲の反応を気にする・職場：上司や同僚に褒められないと落ち込む、必要以上に謝る、评価や顔色を過剰に気にしてしまう・SNS：投稿への反応（いいね・コメント）の数や有無に一喜一憂しやすいこれらはいずれも「拒絶されたくない」「認められたい」という不安型特有の欲求が、恋愛以外の対人関係にも波及している例だといえます。────────────────────7．メンタルヘルスへの影響────────────────────・224の研究をまとめたメタ分析では、愛着不安（attachment anxiety）が不安症状や抑うつ、孤独感の高さと関連していることが示されています。・不安型・回避型のいずれも、抑うつ・不安症状と正の相関があることが複数の研究で確認されています。・不安型愛着は、うつ病のリスクを高めるという指摘や、若年層における不安症状のリスク上昇と関連するという研究報告もあります。・愛着スタイルは心理的な問題だけでなく、慢性的なストレス反応・炎症・免疫機能の低下など、身体的な健康とも関連する可能性が指摘されています。────────────────────8．境界性パーソナリティ障害（BPD）との関係────────────────────不安型（特に恐れ・回避型／無秩序型）の愛着は、境界性パーソナリティ障害（BPD）や複雑性PTSDと症状が重なりやすいことが知られています。子ども期に虐待歴のある女性のPTSD関連症状を分析した研究では、BPD群には「見捨てられまいとする尋常でない努力」「理想化と脱価値化の間を揺れ動く不安定で激しい対人関係」「不安定な自己感覚・イメージ」「衝動性」といった特徴が、複雑性PTSDと共通する「自己組織化の障害」に加えて認められたと報告されています。ただし、不安型愛着そのものはパーソナリティ障害の診断基準を満たすものではなく、多くの場合は「傾向」として理解されるべきものです。症状が重く生活に支障が出ている場合は、自己判断で結論を出さず、精神科・心療内科での相談が推奨されます。────────────────────9．統計データ────────────────────海外の調査・メタ分析からは、以下のような数値が報告されています（調査によって数値には幅があります）。・成人の愛着スタイルの分布について、あるメタ分析（約30研究）では安定型が約51％前後とされています。別の全国調査では安定型が約56％、不安型（とらわれ型）が約19％、回避型が約25％という報告もあります。・1997年の全国調査では、回避型が約25％、不安型が約11％、残りが恐れ回避型／無秩序型に分類されたと報告されています。・1万件以上の成人愛着面接（AAI）を対象にした2009年のメタ分析（Bakermans-Kranenburg & van IJzendoorn）では、非臨床群において拒絶型（回避型）が約23％、とらわれ型（不安型）が約19％という、比較的近い割合が確認されています。・安定型の人は、不安定型に比べて関係満足度が高いとする調査結果もあります。・不安型愛着は、追跡調査において交際relationshipの破局率の高さと関連するという報告もあります。これらの数値は調査対象や測定方法によって差があるため、あくまで目安として捉えてください。────────────────────10．克服・改善に向けたアプローチ────────────────────不安型愛着は、幼少期の経験によって形成されたものであっても、固定されたものではなく、大人になってからでも変化させることが可能だとされています。心理学ではこれを「earned secure attachment（獲得された安定型愛着）」と呼びます。成人愛着面接では、つらい子ども時代の経験を一貫性・バランスを持って語れるかどうかで、この「獲得された安定型」を判別するとされています。【セルフケアでできること】・自己理解を深める：自分がどんな場面で不安が強くなるのか、パターンを客観的に把握する・自分を責めないこと：不安型の傾向は「性格の欠陥」ではなく学習されたパターンであると理解する・自分軸を持つ：他人からの評価に依存せず、自分自身の価値観や興味に基づいて行動する・夢中になれるものを見つける：仕事や趣味など、自分自身のライフワークを持つことが安心感の土台になる・一人の時間に慣れる練習をする・感情を率直に、かつ落ち着いた形で相手に伝える練習をする・パートナーに変化を強要しないこと：変えられるのは自分自身であって相手ではない【専門的な治療・カウンセリング】・カウンセリング／心理療法：なぜ不安になるのかを、安全な環境の中で見つめ直すプロセス。専門家に助けを求めること自体が「安心を育てる練習」になるとも言われます。・認知行動療法（CBT）：不安を強める思考パターンに焦点を当て、修正していくアプローチ・感情焦点化療法（EFT／Emotionally Focused Therapy）：カップルセラピーとして特に研究が進んでおり、パートナー同士が「追う－逃げる」といった負の悪循環のパターンを特定し、新しい情緒的な関わり方を築くことを目指します。複数の研究で、EFTはおよそ70〜75％のカップルに改善効果があったと報告されています。・アタッチメントに基づく心理療法（Attachment-Based Therapy）、AEDP（加速化体験力動療法）、DDP（対話的発達心理療法）などの手法も、愛着トラウマの回復に用いられます。・EMDR：トラウマ処理を目的とした治療法で、愛着トラウマやPTSD症状の軽減に用いられることがあります。・弁証法的行動療法（DBT）：感情調整のスキルを学ぶうえで役立つとされています。・投薬：不安障害や抑うつ症状を伴う場合、心療内科・精神科での薬物療法が検討されることもあります。【変化にかかる時間】多くの資料で共通して指摘されているのは、変化には時間がかかるという点です。セラピーによる初期の自己認識・感情調整の改善は3〜6か月程度で感じられ始めることが多い一方、安定した「獲得された安定型愛着」を築くまでには、半年〜数年、場合によっては1〜3年程度の継続的な取り組みが必要とされています。焦らず、一進一退を前提に取り組むことが勧められています。【挫折しないためのポイント】・「すぐ治る」と期待しすぎない・完璧を目指さない：後退する日があっても自分を責めない・一つの方法にこだわらない：セルフケアとカウンセリングなど複数を組み合わせる方が効果的とされる・つらいときは一人で抱え込まず、早めに専門家に相談する────────────────────11．よくある関連キーワード────────────────────内的作業モデル／安全基地／ストレンジ・シチュエーション法／成人愛着面接（AAI）／ECR尺度／とらわれ型愛着／アンビバレント型愛着／見捨てられ不安／試し行動／共依存／複雑性PTSD／毒親／愛着の世代間連鎖／獲得された安定型愛着（earned secure attachment）────────────────────参考・出典（クリックで開けます）────────────────────https://psychotherapy.jp/anxious-attachment-characteristics-improvement-methods/https://sanyokai-clinic.com/kokoro/8121/https://katsushikabashi.jp/article/huangata-aichakushougai/https://fire-method.com/tomoshibi/column_tomoshibi/anxious-attachment/https://blog.mylifenote.ai/ja/attachment-types-ja/https://coconala.com/blogs/2307087/319136https://attachment-kou.jp/%E3%80%8C%E4%B8%8D%E5%AE%89%E5%9E%8B%E6%84%9B%E7%9D%80%E3%82%B9%E3%82%BF%E3%82%A4%E3%83%AB%E3%80%8D%E3%81%A8%E3%81%AF/https://shirokuma-co.com/column/attachment-style-counseling/https://kashiwa-ekimae.com/media/column-fuangata-aichaku-naoshikata/https://mental-therapy.com/huan-kyohu/https://akasakacl.com/fuan-gata-aichaku-shogai/https://cocorac-clinic.com/blog/how-to-care-for-attachment-disorderhttps://my-career.shop/cure/https://www.kitanodai.jp/column/attachment-disorder/https://mental-cocoromi-cl.jp/blog/13965https://www.brieftherapy-counseling.com/attachment-4-6602.htmlhttps://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%84%9B%E7%9D%80%E7%90%86%E8%AB%96https://psychologist.x0.com/terms/142.htmlhttps://psychotherapy.jp/attachment-theory-bowlby-explained/https://sw.self-sufficiency.jp/attachment/https://cocololabo.com/blog1/psychology-bowlby/https://www.docswell.com/s/matsuzaki_asaki/57V6Q8-2023-11-13-183108https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/25170-attachment-styleshttps://www.attachmentproject.com/blog/anxious-attachment/https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/addiction-and-recovery/202009/recognizing-the-anxious-attachment-stylehttps://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/manners-of-relating/202311/dealing-with-adult-anxious-preoccupied-attachment-stylehttps://therapygroupdc.com/therapist-dc-blog/anxious-attachment-101-what-it-is-how-it-shows-up-and-how-to-get-anxious-attachment-help/https://missionconnectionhealthcare.com/mental-health/attachment-disorder/anxious-attachment-style/https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5319988/https://wifitalen items.body: Run by our very own Joseph Sannicandro, the Lost Children Net Label has been quiet as a Bandcamp imprint, but kept alive through Joseph’s podcasts and newsletter posts since the 2022 release of the massive 56-track [Useless Sounds]. Returning in full force with a triptych of tapes, Lost Children is ready to reclaim its place at the forefront of experimental music. The crown jewel of the bundle is CRACKS, a gathering of international musicians who address the “concept of the border as a colonial wound.” Proceeds benefit the Council on American-Islamic Relations Minnesota and Lumpen Radio (an initiative of the Public Media Institute in Chicago). The confrontational words on the cover have become a global rallying cry. Joni Void starts the set off with “Borders,” cutting right to the chase. The percussion sounds like a jailer’s baton dragged across prison bars. A connection is made between physical borders, sonic borders and the borders of perception, with dialogue interrupted by the siren and blare of a local enforcement agent. Martín Rodríguez shares radio transmissions heard from the Arizona-Mexico border where he was raised, giving credit to radio for helping him to recover from a brain tumor. The transmissions sparkle and fade, as if underlining the name of the Lost Children imprint. One thinks of voices and souls lost and the search for missing loved ones, possibly deported, possibly dead. Kate Carr offers bucolic bells bisected by the essential chaos of street protests, suggesting that the comfortable must be disturbed in order for substantive change to unfold. Lubo Alexandrov‘s bucolic “Echoes (from the other side)” doesn’t identify which side it refers to, leaving the interpretation wide open. Speaker Music‘s haunting, echoed, abraded and ultimately percussive “Moral Injury” exposes the deepest rupture of the crisis as an affront to goodness itself. Sannicandro’s own “rethink not reform” brings the sound to the streets, the appealing “Wait” of an electronic crossing signal contrasted with a sense that the fragile peace is about to be disturbed; in layers of increasing ferocity, it is. The disorientation of the intimate soundscape imitates that of the assaulted. apartment52‘s “i would die for anything, maybe” exposes a different insecurity while repeating the effect of messages that fail to get through. A heartfelt live recording from Hamza Lahmadi connects the yearning of sojourners around the world, who just want a place to call home. Mai Mai Mai incorporates waves as siren call, implying both the hope of welcome and the lack of permission to land. The drone is lonely and isolated, the land right there. Anas Hajam lightens the mood a bit with finger-picking goodness and breath; one needs encouragement such as this. Then Joni Void returns as the remixer of Soledad Rosas‘ “Piel,” which extends the references to breath along with vocal glissandos and tender song. The intake just prior to the second minute recalls George Floyd. Only a minute long, Esther B.‘s “molti sport” is a rush of static awaiting definition. Then comes a reference to Greek mythology: thenewobjective feat. Cole Pulice use “Scylla and Charybdis” to reference the idiom “the lesser of two evils,” summarizing the current state of border disputes, in which no one wins. Stefan Christoff closes the compilation with “Turn,” whose tolling church bells, echoed on prepared piano, are both indictment and call to arms. Two artists featured on CRACKS also branch out across the bundle. ATMOSPHERICS is taken from a series of soundscape broadcasts prepared by Diana Duta & Stefan Christoff. Partially recorded on the silver anniversary of Portugal’s Carnation Revolution, “Paysage sonare” is a tribute to victory, a long battle finally won. The sounds of the coast are sounds of peace in both senses of the word. Soft ambient tones unify the composition, wresting control from the field recordings in the tenth minute before ceding space in the eighteenth and again in the thirty-first, ending in familial laughter and joy. Similar sounds launch the title track, recorded in Brussels. The piece eventually branches into the northern marshes, calling on hydrophones for a glance below the surface. The contrast between city and marsh recalls CRACKS: the discussion of desirable environments, “migration, political dissent and resistance.” The link becomes overt in the chants of the twenty-first minute. Again Christoff’s synth, along with pensive guitar, is the glue that holds the work together, although even this is lost in time, rescued from older tapes, a subtle metaphor. In the long aquatic segment that closes the piece, one feels retreat and resolution. Esther B. is also Esther Bourdages, whose cassette Listening session, live concerts, figure skating “turns the turntable into a destructive instrument.” These live improvisations expose the turntable as preserver and destroyer of memory. Segments rise through the ether intact, only to be savaged with love. There’s a huge difference between turntablism in a hip-hop sense and turntablism in an experimental sense, but the two are not exclusive. In her preference for the older, even archival records, Bourdages honors The Caretaker; in her disdain for the creation of linear narratives or danceable samples, she honors Kid Koala. “figure skating” flips the script, conflating the stylus and the skate, the vinyl and the ice, with few if any identifiable markers until the end: a mesmerizing lesson in abstraction and a companion to Curling. In “Earache, My Eye,” a horrified son protests to his father, “You ruined my record, man!” Such a thing does not exist in Bourdages’ world, where records are purposely altered by “grinding, cutting and sanding.” If anything, the imperfections are the draw. Yet it is obvious that the artist loves her collection, teasing sounds from these records that were never intended to be heard, like coaxing stories from a childhood friend. It is passing strange to hear them on a cassette, although in the hands of another this might be manipulated in a different way, then passed to a digital specialist for further dismantling. We once thought that sound, once recorded, was fixed; we believe so no longer. Welcome back, Lost Children! (Richard Allen)

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Gianni Leone has remained active since the era of YS, the album for which he is best remembered, and it was in this spirit that Il Balletto di Bronzo returned to craft a highly distinctive work. Rich in nuance and imagery, it evokes a dark, ominous, and theatrical atmosphere; performing as a trio, the band ingeniously constructs a soundscape that suggests specific moods and settings, scenes suspended in time and space where the very concepts of time and space begin to lose their meaning."Oceani Sconosciuti" carries an air of silent-film horror reminiscent of the band Crucis, while the atonal counterpoint found throughout the album also shares common ground with the music of Van Der Graaf Generator. Gianni handles the vocals, lending Lemures a distinct avant-garde aura."L'Emofago" features a powerful drum foundation reminiscent of Led Zeppelin; the atmosphere created by the keyboards and the lyrics of this concept �lbum, which incorporates symphonic Minimoog flourishes and operatic recitatives within a hard rock (bordering on heavy metal) context, complements Gianni's soaring vocals. It evokes lightning bolts and tremors raining down upon Sodom and Gomorrah, all delivered by the trio in this magnificent progressive work. It suggests that the best of the 70s never truly faded away; rather, updated for the present, that spirit remains more vital than ever, especially since the music avoids sounding merely "vintage."Napoli Sotterranea paints vivid mental images, an entire movie, really. Keyboards take on the role of guitars, while the vocals explore mystical Eastern melodies, accompanied by a drum and bass foundation that occasionally borders on psychedelia before embracing jazz-rock, though of a violent, provocative, and aggressive variety. This is not the comeback of an established band merely recreating the past; rather, it is a group intent on offering something new and making a fresh contribution to the musical landscape.There is melody in L'Ombra Degli Dei... ideas are laid out; it is music that is alive, in the tradition of Italian progressive rock, drawing upon its influences to forge something new. Following a keyboard introduction, an instrumental section transports us into a different world; each step of the staircase leads to a distinct realm. "Labyrinthus" blends Eddie Jobson's U.K.-style keyboards with Gianni Leone's operatic vocals, while a jazz section with a Canterbury-esque spirit permeates the entire piece; the trio delivers an impeccable performance, featuring an improvised section where time constraints seem irrelevant, that evokes a chamber-music atmosphere, ultimately allowing that blend of tragic and futuristic romanticism to return and take hold.The intricate, agile keyboard arrangements of "Certezze Fragili" contrast with the dense, suspended atmosphere of "Deliquio Viola," where this progressive-opera fusion is pushed to its absolute limits, akin to reconstructing a Renaissance past using parts from dismantled cars. They achieve the seemingly impossible; all that remains is to follow the rhythm as the keyboards and drums, pulsing with energy, lead us to "Il Vento Poi." There, echoes of the wind sweep the voices away, distorting them and blurring the lines between reality and time, exposing their relativity, and, by extension, their malleability, as well as the possibility of altering them through perception.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — The man who would fall to Earth in 1976 never truly stayed in one place; London, Detroit, Los Angeles, and Berlin always hosted him merely as a temporary traveler, a restless tenant destined to leave sooner or later. It was in this context that, after bidding farewell to Ziggy Stardust, he moved forward with that same band, featuring Mick Ronson, Trevor Bolder, and Mick Woodmansey, but also Ken Fordham on sax, three backing vocalists, and Mike Garson on piano, whose contribution would make all the difference.Naturally, lessons with Lindsay Kemp, the British dancer, actor, mime, choreographer, and set designer, helped shape the persona of Aladdin Sane, a character that offered a critique of the entertainment world and was inspired by the very tour during which the songs comprising the album were written.That same dichotomy, between the lightning bolt across his face and his stance regarding his newfound stardom, ultimately extended to the music itself; one can distinguish between Rolling Stones-esque blues-soul rockers like "Watch That Man," "Panic in Detroit," "Cracked Actor," a fast-paced glam version of "Let's Spend the Night Together," and "The Jean Genie," and other, more experimental tracks. The latter reveal the jazz-inflected and at times atonal influence of Mike Garson, as well as a cabaret DNA and darker, more evocative, compositionally complex themes, songs like "Aladdin Sane (1913-1938-197?)," "Time" (heavily influenced by Jacques Brel, an essential reference for understanding one of his earthly personas), "The Prettiest" (evoking the 1950s, a style that kept coming and going), and "Lady Grinning," a gem featuring a flamenco-style introduction. Both Mick Ronson on guitar and Mike Garson on piano earned their pivotal roles in creating that special magic, an artistic expression that would eventually lead him to portray Paul Ambrosius von Przygodski in the 1978 film Just a Gigolo: a young Prussian character drifting between two worlds yet finding a true home in neither, never fully belonging, much like Aladdin Sane.

You will search in vain for rhythms and harmonies here, of course; "Gold" is an album of free form. It chirps, pings and creaks merrily away; only in track 12 (the tracks have no titles) does something almost akin to a dance mood arise as a result of the electronic percussion; although even to this you can hardly dance, there is simply too much going on. An oriental-sounding flute improvises over heavy chirping and bubbling above the quasi-soloing percussion. Space techno? With the following track, "13", which sounds like a cool, empty factory hall turned into music, a bit of Industrial also comes into play."Gold" is fun and enormously entertaining for those people who (like me) find many of the productions of the "Berlin School" incredibly boring. Not a typical Conrad Schnitzler album, but for me (perhaps for that very reason) one of the best.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — ProjeKct Three's 'Masque' comes straight from the R&D department of King Crimson. This is the thirdinstallment in the live project series featuring members of the 'THRAK' lineup of the Robert Fripp-led band, brought together with the aim of exploring off-beat ideas through improvisation andexperimentation. These are live recordings featuring alternating lineups of the 90s Crimson, withthis particular 1999 recording featuring the trio of Robert Fripp, Trey Gunn, and Pat Mastelotto. Asis the case with the majority of the KC releases from that period, the music played by ProjeKctThree incorporates the spacey ambient soundscapes patented by Fripp, together with the finely tunedWarr guitar of Trey Gunn and the impressive array of electronic percussion and loops played by PatMastelotto. The type of experimental rock presented on 'Masque', however, is more abstract and lessgroovy than the output of other ProjeKcts (like One or Two, which makes it closer to something like'Thrakattak' than the album 'THRAK' itself.The thirteen tracks making up this live album are numbered and (perhaps suggestively) left untitled,while the somewhat intimidating, surreal and impersonal cover art uncannily reflects the kind ofmusic played on 'Masque'. This is one of these experimental recordings that only make sense whenheard in their entirety, but if I were to outline several pieces of greater significance, I wouldhave to start with '1', which is an obnoxious and impulsive opener, replete with hefty bass tonesand obscure guitar licks. 'Masque 2' then presents a more sustained rock sound tinted with gentleambient soundscapes, while the complex rhythms on '3' weave around the haunting electronics in arather menacing way. Later on, 'Masque 7' represents another abstract-sided piece, impressing with asoft but prominent bass sound, whereas the industrial hue encompassing 'Masque 8' makes it one ofthe darker compositions heard on this album. It is also worth noting how effective the hypnoticallyabrasive sounds on '9' are, with the two final pieces also being among the highlights.Of all the ProjeKcts, Three might be the single most intriguing variation of Crimson - 'Masque' isunorthodox and compelling, but for me this is the kind of experimentation that drives the genreforward.

items.body: Impressed by this partnership’s Dvořák Ninth (review), I was eager to hear their Bruckner fourth, surely the composer’s most popular symphony both in the concert hall and on record. This new reading, while impressive, is not a complete success. Symphony No. 4 Amazon Presto Apple This reading lacks the instrumental weight and depth of color that I would argue makes for an authentic Bruckner sound. Having grown up listening to many Telarc recordings of this orchestra, I lay the blame for this deficiency on the engineering. The mics are placed too close to the musicians, surely to minimize audience noise during this live recording. There is little bloom to the sound, and no real hall ambience. Climaxes feel contained, and softer dynamics are limited by the proximity of the mics. Bruckner’s music was written with a warm, reverberant acoustic in mind, and that acoustic is an integral part of the sound. Not so here. Instead, it is like standing one foot away from Seurat’s A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte: every brush stroke is visible, and we might appreciate how the painting is assembled, but it comes at the cost of the image’s beauty, mystery and expression. The second issue has to do with the edition. There are now ten different editions of the fourth symphony to choose from. Stutzmann uses the late Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs’ 2021 critical edition of the 1878–81 version, which has been recorded only once before, by Simon Rattle with the LSO (LSO Live). For that album Cohrs described his edition as “the second version of the ‘Romantic’ Symphony as it stood by the end of 1881,” including “Bruckner’s own suggested cut in the Finale.” But Stutzmann does not take the cut — why not? Why embrace a little-known version and then ignore one of its most significant, composer-sanctioned changes? The liner notes offer no discussion of the edition, nor is it listed on either side of the booklet cover. As to the performance itself, I had initially intended to limit comparisons to other American recordings, but it now seems best to set Stutzmann against Rattle (details – review). His performance is faster, with an overall timing of 61’30” against Stutzmann’s 71’39”, and the largest difference comes in the final movement, where Stutzmann restores the passage Bruckner marked for cutting. Each conductor belongs to a different interpretive school. Rattle recalls Karajan: a subtle use of rubato, polished orchestral sound with resplendent brass and gossamer strings, a unified pulse that keeps the structure in view. Stutzmann is far closer to Jochum: much freer rubato, a more heterogeneous orchestral sound and, more distinctively, an intensely songful rendering of Bruckner’s score. Nathalie Stutzmann conducts the Atlanta Symphony Orchestra. Photo © Rand Lines. Stutzmann’s approach is compelling in the second movement, though at 17’05” it feels more Adagio than Bruckner’s Andante quasi Allegretto. In the finale the flexibility sometimes compromises a sense of the overarching structure, and there are moments when the energy level dips precipitously low. This is less of an issue in the opening movement, where one does get to hear much of the contrapuntal inner voices. Both Rattle and Stutzmann solicit rounded articulation, and I often missed the cut and thrust of Blomstedt’s San Francisco account on Decca and Honeck’s Pittsburgh performance on Reference, especially in the Scherzo. Both drive the music harder, encouraging more wildness in the trumpet-capped climaxes. Bruckner described the Trio as “how a barrel-organ plays during the midday meal in the forest.” Honeck is perhaps best at capturing this rustic picture, even if he is reticent to allow an earthier, less refined sound. Stutzmann conjures a poised, lightly sprung elegance that I enjoyed, even though it hardly captures the composer’s description. In short, I find Stutzmann’s performance the more compelling of the two. Yet if I want to hear this edition, surely I want Bruckner’s cut in the finale. Rattle’s release adds to the symphony itself the discarded 1874/76 Scherzo and the 1878 Volksfest Finale, an extended early version of the Andante, and the unabridged 1881 Finale, a valuable addition for Bruckner specialists. Ultimately, neither recording compels me to embrace this version over the more familiar Haas and Nowak editions, and neither matches the brilliance of Blomstedt, Honeck, or the classic Böhm/Vienna/Decca. items.body: Mitsuko Uchida’s 2025 live performance of the late Beethoven sonatas (Op. 109–111) arrives almost two decades after her studio recording for Decca, and it carries the added weight of being her final account of these works. Her choice of Suntory Hall marks a homecoming: she has played there since the hall’s opening season in 1986, and remains its only Associate Artist. Last Three Sonatas Amazon Presto Apple The gap between the two readings naturally raises the question of how much her interpretations have developed. If we go by Op. 109, things have indeed changed: not a drastic pivot, but an amplification of certain aspects. The 2006 reading already had an appreciable fluidity, but in the newer Vivace (track 1) Uchida makes more unabashed pauses and rubatos that still fit naturally into the music. Some of the urgency of the earlier second movement has turned into greater dramatic power here, and the attention to articulation and secondary voices is never sacrificed. The temperament of the final movement (track 3) can vary considerably depending on the tempo of the opening theme. Where Serkin and Gilels move more slowly and evoke contemplation, Uchida is brisker than either of them, and her pace captures the cantabile of Beethoven’s marking. In the variations that follow, a deep familiarity reveals itself in her ability to balance forward motion against the emphasis the grandest moments need. Op. 110 comes alive through contrast. Uchida uses Beethoven’s textures to shift between lyricism and resonance. The arpeggios at the start of the Moderato cantabile (track 4), leading up to the second theme, are a prime example: they begin as shimmering filigree and morph into a resplendent presence — perhaps a fitting representation of the vocal and orchestral sides she brings out throughout. The Scherzo carries a much higher degree of austerity and insistence than the 2006 Decca version, though both readings remain entirely valid. The Adagio (track 6) reveals a performer who understands the profundity of late Beethoven: the desperation, the melancholy with its sharp poignancy, the gravitas of internal conflict and weariness. What is most captivating is her ability to convey the rawness of these sentiments in a live setting. Uchida’s Fuga (track 7) proves more multidimensional than many. The switch from minor to major is subtle, and it gives her room to explore the quieter sides of the fugue before it spins into something much larger. Even in the softest playing nothing sounds hurried. Pauses are placed to maximize dynamic contrast while delineating the intricacies of Beethoven’s structure. Mitsuko Uchida. Photo © Justin Pumfrey / Decca. Although it moves slightly slower at times than her previous interpretation, the new Op. 111 (tracks 8–9) embodies the severity and boldness of the Maestoso marking. The urgency of the prior account has developed into an equally compelling adamance. The calmness of the Arietta feels like an arrival after a long journey. The same weighty substance carries into the variations, which works for the most part, though the syncopated variation at 6’40” could take a touch more rhythmic vitality. What emerges most strongly, though, is the intricacy of the tender moments, which linger in their transcendence. The engineers have kept audience noise to a minimum, and the piano is captured with enough clarity to register its tone and regulation. As a final account of these sonatas this is a distinguished one, and the culmination of Uchida’s long engagement with them. items.body: Saint-Saëns completed his Symphony No. 3 in 1886, commissioned by the Philharmonic Society of London, and conducted the premiere himself at the age of fifty. It was the last symphony he would write, and it came at the height of his career. He is said to have remarked that he would never achieve anything like it again. When Franz Liszt died later that year, Saint-Saëns dedicated the score to his memory. The “Organ” nickname is a little misleading. The composer wrote not a concerto but a symphony “with organ,” where the instrument works inside the orchestra rather than in front of it. The scoring also calls for a piano, played at times by two players. The four traditional movements are folded into two continuous parts, unified by a single theme that keeps returning in new forms, a technique absorbed from Liszt. The music travels from restless C minor to a blazing C major finale, whose massive organ entrance has tested engineers as much as conductors. Recordings have answered that challenge in different ways, from concert-hall organs captured in place to a cathedral instrument recorded separately and mixed in. Here are The Classic Review editorial team’s recommendations for the best recordings of Saint-Saëns’s Symphony No. 3 (“Organ”). Boston Symphony Orchestra, Charles Munch More than sixty years after it was made, Charles Munch’s 1959 recording in Boston remains the one to beat. The thrill comes from playing of scorching intensity that unfolds like a live concert. Munch sets a fast tempo for the first movement’s main theme, and the rhythmic drive never lets up. The strings sing the *Poco adagio* with unforced lyricism, a reminder that this performance is not all fire. In the finale, Berj Zamkochian’s organ makes a thunderous entrance, its bass seeming to shake the floor. The aging tape strains audibly under that huge chord, yet the drama sweeps this flaw aside. Add Munch’s Debussy *La Mer* and Ibert *Escales* as couplings, and the disc’s legendary status is easy to understand. Munch Amazon Presto Apple Chicago Symphony Orchestra, Daniel Barenboim The organ heard on Daniel Barenboim’s 1976 Chicago recording was played an ocean away from the orchestra. Gaston Litaize recorded his part on the organ of Chartres Cathedral, and the two performances were joined afterward in the studio. That procedure could easily have sounded artificial, but the combined result has an epic, almost otherworldly presence. It crowns a performance of irresistible panache, with the Chicago brass playing at full strength and a finale of colossal impact. Barenboim’s invigorating first-movement tempo leaves the strings a little untidy in places, a small price for the sweep he achieves. It matches Munch for voltage while sounding far more modern. For the symphony’s raw physical thrill, this is the version to reach for. Barenboim Amazon Presto Apple Detroit Symphony Orchestra, Paul Paray Paul Paray’s 1957 Detroit account moves with exceptional lightness. Its appeal is not weight or blaze, but transparency and grace. Paray trained this orchestra himself, and it shows in the supple phrasing and the way every strand stays audible. Tempos are bracingly fast, yet nothing feels rushed. The playing stays composed even at full speed. The organ part is in the hands of Marcel Dupré, one of the great virtuosos of the twentieth century. Made with just three microphones, the recording remains astonishingly fresh for its age, clearer than Munch’s. For listeners who want to hear the elegance inside this symphony, Paray is the essential alternative. Paray Amazon Presto Apple Montreal Symphony Orchestra, Charles Dutoit Few discs did more to show off the young CD format than Charles Dutoit’s 1982 Montreal recording. Its lasting virtues, though, are musical: elastic, beautifully controlled phrasing and orchestral playing of rare polish. Peter Hurford’s organ is cleanly focused and never distorts, even in the loudest pages. Every detail sits in natural proportion. The coupling is the Second Piano Concerto, with Pascal Rogé as soloist. Those who crave the sheer force of Munch or Barenboim may find Dutoit reserved. Anyone meeting the symphony for the first time could not ask for a better guide. Dutoit Amazon Presto Apple Kansas City Symphony, Michael Stern Glorious sound is the first thing anyone notices about Michael Stern’s 2013 recording with the Kansas City Symphony. It is not, however, the main reason to recommend the album. The performance underneath has genuine vitality, with crisp rhythms and the rich, full-bodied sonority this music thrives on. Jan Kraybill presides over a big Casavant concert organ, and the recording gives it impressive depth and space. The couplings are generous: the *Introduction and Rondo capriccioso* with violinist Noah Geller, and the lesser-known *La Muse et le Poète*. A performance this alive earns its place beside the classics. Stern Amazon Presto Apple Top image ©️ The Classic Review, AI generated The form can be filled in the actual website url. items.body: The members of the Norwegian trio Tazer introduce themselves only by their aliases: ‘CALICO’, ‘ONI-X01’, and ‘DRUMNIBAL’. Beyond that, they prefer to keep an air of mystery – something I won’t attempt to unravel here. Their focus is on the music rather than the people behind it, and rightly so. I first discovered Tazer through their earlier EP, but it is their self-released debut album, “Taze Is The Rule”, that truly demands attention. It has been a long time since a debut record has hit me with this kind of force. This is pure sonic aggression, forged from a relentless fusion of EBM, Metal, and Techno. Every track is crushingly heavy, leaving nothing standing in its wake. The songs strike with the intensity of an imaginary war machine, determined to conquer dark dance floors and every poor soul brave enough to step onto them. Tazer sounds like an explosion whose full impact has yet to be measured. Fortunately, the band took the time to answer a few questions and shed some light on the ideas, influences, and vision behind “Taze Is The Rule”. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Tazer ‘Taze Is The Rule’ interview Q: Let’s start by clearing up a few things: where do Tazer and the project’s name come from? Who is behind the aliases, and what has your musical journey been like up to this point? CALICO: The Tazer project officially kicked off in 2024 when we wrote our first EP, “9001 Volts”. We chose the name Tazer because we wanted something that felt high-voltage but was also instantly recognizable. A small taser can pack a massive punch, and that just felt like the perfect metaphor for our energy. As for our aliases, they are symbols. Honestly, who we are behind them really doesn’t matter, we are our music, and we prefer to let the tracks do the talking. Q: What have been the key influences and sources of inspiration behind your music, and what does this particular form of expression mean to you? ONI-X01: We’ve always been massive fans of bands like Rammstein and Combichrist, but we really wanted to inject our own flavor into the mix. The goal was to create something heavy and raw, but also immediate and danceable. By mixing Metal with classic EBM elements, we want to hit people right in the gut and pull them into a completely new kind of mindset. Q: How did this debut album come together, and how were the songwriting and production responsibilities divided among the band members? Looking back, what were the biggest challenges you faced while creating it? DRUMNIBAL: This album is the result of years of hard work. Out of the 10 tracks we originally wrote, 5 of them ended up on the “9001 Volts” EP. So, over the next two years, we had to write 5 brand-new tracks to bring the album back to 10. During that time, our sound naturally evolved and the line-up shifted into the trio we are today. Our creative process is pretty organic: we usually start with electronic riffs, build a solid structure, and then layer on the guitars, bass, and vocals. Lyrics always come last because they depend entirely on the vibe and emotion the music triggers in us. We write everything together as a team, no strict division of labor, just pure collaboration. Q: If I understand correctly, “Taze Is The Rule” is more than just an album title – it also serves as a kind of manifesto for the band. Both lyrically and musically, the track comes across as hard-hitting, provocative, and uncompromising. Could you elaborate on that? What does it reveal about your perspective on the world and the society we live in? ONI-X01: You hit the nail on the head. “Taze Is The Rule” is our manifesto, our creed, and our undeniable truth. It all started with this first track, which really opened our eyes and made us realize exactly what we wanted to create. We feel like the world is lacking a bit of discipline right now; everything seems to get lost in superficial noise and trivial complaints that don’t really lead anywhere. That’s why we felt the need to forge music that brings back some of that discipline, giving people an ideal to rally behind with a sound that’s tough, but fair. Q: Both your music and visual identity seem perfectly suited for the live stage. What have your experiences been like so far, and what can audiences expect from a Tazer performance? DRUMNIBAL: Throughout our musical journeys, we’ve spent enough time on stage to consider ourselves live veterans. However, with this specific project, we are completely rethinking our approach to live shows to deliver something genuinely fresh and powerful. We know it’s a challenge, ‘cause the live scene is incredibly competitive right now, and coming up with original ideas takes a lot of the discipline we talk about. We apply that same focus to our music videos, carefully crafting our identity through every choice of makeup, wardrobe, storyline, and camera angle. Q: Are you already working on new material or perhaps even a follow-up album? Do you have a clear vision of how Tazer will evolve in the future and where you would like to take the project? CALICO: We definitely have a long-term plan, which includes diving into a second album. We already have some ideas cooking that we hope people will love. Right now, though, the main focus of that plan is locking down and developing our live shows. We honestly can’t wait to bring these tracks to the stage and connect with the crowd under the banner of ‘Taze is the Rule’. About Tazer Tazer is a Norwegian electro-industrial project formed in 2024 by musicians performing under the aliases CALICO, ONI-X01, and DRUMNIBAL, and signed to Hellektrokution Records. The band debuted with the single “A Razor Can Slit, A Tazer Can Kill” on 5 November 2024, followed by the self-released EP “9001 Volts” on 21 December 2024. Of the ten tracks the band had written by then, five appeared on that EP; the remaining five, plus five newly written tracks, became the ten-track debut album “Taze Is The Rule”, released via Hellektrokution Records on 30 April 2026. The album combines EBM, industrial metal and techno, with influences including Rammstein and Combichrist. Tazer returned in October 2025 with a Halloween video for “I Put a Spell on You”, and in May 2026 released the single “Raise The Voltage”, the album’s fifth track, via Hellektrokution Records, Spotify, YouTube and Bandcamp. The band is now focused on developing a live show and has begun writing material for a second album.

items.body: YouTube creator marceve76 has reimagined a-ha‘s 1985 debut album “Hunting High and Low” as if it had been recorded in the 1950s, complete with a mock cover picturing the trio as “The A-Has” in period suits and pompadours. The video, titled “A-Ha – Hunting High And Low, if it was recorded in the 50s,” runs 30 minutes and 20 seconds and covers the album’s full ten-track sequence, including “Take On Me.” The video was already uploaded on November 10, 2025, and has drawn 5,345 views so far. Not a lot that is, despite being one of the better produced videos on his channel, musically speaking. The vocal performance is not Morten Harket’s, and the channel is upfront about the nature of the project, opening with a disclaimer that “voices, faces and characters have no connection to actual people”, and that “the video is an artistic and transformative work made for entertainment purposes.” A recurring format built around AI reinterpretation marceve76 runs a 51,900-subscriber channel built almost entirely around reimagining well-known albums as 1950s recordings, a format that leans on AI music generation, voice and style transfer. Side-Line covered the same creator’s take on Depeche Mode’s “Violator” in July 2025. The “Hunting High and Low” video sits in the same catalog alongside similar treatments of Fleetwood Mac’s “Rumours,” Blondie’s “Parallel Lines,” David Bowie’s “Let’s Dance,” Led Zeppelin’s debut, Dio’s “Holy Diver” and AC/DC’s “The Razors Edge,” among others. The full “Hunting High and Low” tracklist covered in the video, with timestamps: “Take On Me” – 0:00 “Train of Thought” – 2:52 “Hunting High and Low” – 5:52 “The Blue Sky” – 9:09 “Living a Boy’s Adventure Tale” – 12:18 “The Sun Always Shines on T.V.” – 16:12 “And You Tell Me” – 19:44 “Love Is Reason” – 22:20 “I Dream Myself Alive” – 24:52 “Here I Stand and Face the Rain” – 27:17 About a-ha a-ha formed in Oslo, Norway, in 1982, when vocalist Morten Harket joined songwriters Pål Waaktaar and Magne Furuholmen, who had been playing together in earlier Oslo bands. Signed to Warner Bros., the trio released their debut album, “Hunting High and Low,” on June 1, 1985, in Norway and the United States, followed by a UK and European release on October 28 that year. Its lead single “Take On Me” had first been issued in 1984 without success; a 1985 re-release, paired with Steve Barron’s rotoscope-animated video mixing live action and pencil animation, took the song to number one in 36 countries and won six awards at the 1986 MTV Video Music Awards. “Hunting High and Low” also produced the singles “Love Is Reason,” “The Sun Always Shines on T.V.,” “Train of Thought” and the title track. The album has remained a recurring point of reference for the band’s reissue campaigns: Side-Line reported on a 6LP boxset built around the record in January 2023, and on an exclusive 1984 Demos vinyl pressed for Record Store Day 2025. a-ha went on to release albums including “Scoundrel Days” (1986), “Stay on These Roads” (1988), “East of the Sun, West of the Moon” (1990), “Memorial Beach” (1993), and, after a 2000s reunion, “Analogue” (2005), “Foot of the Mountain” (2009), “Cast in Steel” (2015) and “True North” (2022), the latter accompanied by a documentary film. Side-Line covered the 20th-anniversary reissue of “Analogue” as a 2CD deluxe set with a first-time vinyl pressing in February 2026. In June 2025, Morten Harket revealed a Parkinson’s diagnosis, and Magne Furuholmen discussed the band’s creative process in a Side-Line interview earlier that year. “Take On Me” itself continues to draw new versions from other artists, including a 2025 dark cover by Pure Obsessions & Red Nights.

items.body: English post-punk band The Cure may release their fifteenth studio album in November 2026, according to an unconfirmed report. French fan site Pictures of Cure published the claim on July 31, 2026, citing an unnamed source inside Universal, the band’s distributor, who reportedly listed the album in the company’s release schedule for that month. The report was relayed the same day on the fan forum curefans.com, in its “Unconfirmed news and rumours” section. Neither The Cure, frontman Robert Smith, nor Universal has confirmed a release date. Pictures of Cure ties the November claim to two earlier data points: Smith’s remarks during a BBC Radio 6 Music interview recorded on June 6, 2026, in which he said the album was about to be delivered to the label, and the fact that “Songs of a Lost World,” the record Smith has repeatedly described as this album’s companion piece, was released on November 1, 2024. What Robert Smith has said about the album The Cure returned to Rockfield Studios in Wales in March 2025 to record what Smith has described as three albums’ worth of material. Side-Line reported at the time that 13 songs had been recorded. In the June 2026 BBC Radio 6 Music interview, Smith said the second of those three albums is finished and being delivered to Universal. He called it “more dismal than Songs Of A Lost World” and said it is emotionally connected to that album while approaching the material from a different perspective. A third album, drawn from the same sessions, is “really, really upbeat” and “really poppy,” Smith said, with no indication yet of when it might follow. Two songs earmarked for the upcoming album were named by Smith in January 2025: “It Can Never Be the Same,” a song about grief that the band has performed live for years under the earlier title “Christmas Without You,” and “A Boy I Never Knew,” written during the sessions for The Cure’s 2004 self-titled album. Smith has said the album will also include newer, previously unheard material. “Songs of a Lost World” was released on November 1, 2024, through Fiction Records, ending a 16-year gap since “4:13 Dream” (2008). Produced and mixed by Smith with Paul Corkett and recorded at Rockfield Studios, it was the first Cure album written entirely by Smith and gave the band its first UK number one album in 32 years. About The Cure The Cure formed in Crawley, West Sussex, England, in January 1976, when school friends Robert Smith and Michael Dempsey began playing together, initially under the name Malice. The band went through the name Easy Cure before settling on The Cure and signing to Fiction Records, distributed by Polydor, in 1978. The founding lineup of Smith (guitar, vocals), Dempsey (bass) and Lol Tolhurst (drums) released the debut album “Three Imaginary Boys” in 1979. Through numerous lineup changes, with Smith as the only constant member, The Cure built a catalogue running from the austere post-punk of “Seventeen Seconds” (1980) and “Faith” (1981) through “Pornography” (1982), the pop-facing “The Head on the Door” (1985) and “Kiss Me, Kiss Me, Kiss Me” (1987), to “Disintegration” (1989) and “Wish” (1992), among later releases including “Wild Mood Swings” (1996), “Bloodflowers” (2000), the self-titled “The Cure” (2004) and “4:13 Dream” (2008). The current lineup comprises Robert Smith, Simon Gallup (bass), Roger O’Donnell (keyboards), Jason Cooper (drums) and Reeves Gabrels (guitar). Guitarist and keyboardist Perry Bamonte, who first joined the band in 1984 and rejoined for the “Shows of a Lost World” tour in 2022, died in December 2025 at age 65. The band returned after 16 years away from new albums with “Songs of a Lost World” on November 1, 2024, and confirmed in October 2025 that a follow-up had been recorded at Rockfield Studios. The unconfirmed report of a November 2026 release date would place a new Cure album exactly two years after its predecessor.

items.body: It took the Norwegian duo Kant Kino nearly nine years to release their fourth album. Despite this lengthy hiatus, EBM fans are unlikely to have forgotten the band, as their previous full-length releases were polished, expertly crafted examples of the genre. While EBM remains the album’s primary influence, “Echoes Of The End” also ventures into other sonic territories. The result is a compelling fusion of EBM and Electro-Pop, with occasional touches of Future-Pop. Some tracks recall the melodic approach of Assemblage 23, while the album’s darker moments evoke the early work of Skinny Puppy. At its core, however, “Echoes Of The End” remains a hard-hitting, relentless EBM record, impeccably executed and enriched with vintage-inspired synth textures. The powerful yet controlled vocal delivery perfectly complements the album’s atmosphere. We are treated to no fewer than 24 tracks, although for me the collection is ultimately defined by the irresistible “Choice.” Kant Kino is back—and not a moment too soon. While their sound has evolved, they continue to deliver EBM of the highest caliber. (Rating:8½). Side-Line previously covered the announcement of “Echoes of The End” in April 2026, when the album was confirmed as a digital deluxe edition and a physical 2CD via Alfa Matrix. Listen to “Choice”: Choice by Kant Kino About Kant Kino Kant Kino is a Norwegian electronic duo from Oslo, namely Lars Henrik Madsen and Kenneth Fredstie. The project formed after they wrote a tribute track for the ElektroStat festival, after which a Bunkertracks compilation appearance led to their Alfa Matrix signing. The duo’s debut album, “We Are Kant Kino – You Are Not”, appeared in 2010. It was followed by the “LRSBSS EP” on April 15, 2012, then the second full-length “Father Worked In Industry” on February 22, 2013. “Father Worked In Industry” was mixed and mastered by Claus Larsen of Leaether Strip. That release also produced the download singles “Just For The Comfort Of Sleep EP” on March 26, 2013 and “Ich Liebe Katarina Witt EP” on November 22, 2013. While working toward the third album, the band previewed new material with the teaser “Life” in February 2016. While working on a new album, they self-released the Motörhead/Kraftwerk hybrid “We Are The Roadcrew (Robots)” on December 16, 2016, ahead of “Kopfkino”, which was released on Alfa Matrix on January 13, 2017. In May 2017, Alfa Matrix built the first “Matrix:Reb00ted” volume around Kant Kino remixes. The duo later appeared on the Coldkill vs Kant Kino EP “Silent Morning” in 2018, released the Depeche Mode cover single “Pimpf and Touch Faith” in September 2019, and self-released “Enough! (Demo)” on June 30, 2022. Kenneth Fredstie in the meantime mastered “Face The Beat: Session 3” and Kant Kino contributed “Ich Liebe Katarina Witt (Video Edit)” and “Life (No Fucking Guitars Edit)” to the Face The Beat series. They also contributed a remix for Modulo One’s “No Way to Win”, and remixed the Side-Line charity single “Ukraina” in December 2022. In February 2026, Kant Kino returned with “Rodney: End-State Variations”, followed by the fourth album “Echoes Of The End”, reviewed above.
